body_markdown:
Gooding Christie’s conducted its 22nd Pebble Beach auction this year, bringing 167 vehicles ranging from a 1905 Léon Bollée to historic racers to nearly new Porsches, Lamborghinis, and McLarens. This was the highest-grossing sale in the California-based auction house’s history, and the week’s most expensive car, a Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe, is also the most expensive car Gooding has ever sold.


We were on the ground in Monterey and looked over the most important cars crossing the block during the course of the week. Here, we examine some of the favorites from Gooding Christie’s below.


## Lot 142: 1954 Bentley R-Type Continental


Gooding Christie's


**Sold for $1,215,000**


*Chassis no. BC38LC; Engine no. BCC37. Blue over red leather. Older restoration, #2 condition.*


**Equipment:** LHD. 4.9L straight-six, center-shift four-speed, wheel covers, Flying B hood ornament, driving lights, original radio.


**Condition:** One of 44 LHD cars. Bought new by racer Bill Spear. Damaged in period in an SCCA race, then repaired and fitted with an upgraded 4.9L engine. Bought by Aga Khan in the late 1990s in Switzerland, and a restoration followed. After he died in 2003 he left the car to his chauffeur, who sold it to another Swiss owner in 2004. Further restoration work in 2007 by P&A Wood, and first in class at Pebble Beach in 2009. There are some lightly visible paint cracks above the right headlight and a minuscule chip on the left quarter panel. The mechanical components are immaculate and the underbody merely needs a light detail to look like new again. The interior exhibits minimal wear. A gorgeous old restoration that could pass for a more recent job.


**Bottom line:** This is a very nice car, and the R-Type Continental has one of the best backsides of any automobile ever, but prices for these early ’50s “gentleman’s express” have been sinking significantly over the past year and a half. Gooding’s estimate of “in excess of $2,000,000,” even for a car with such desirable specs (LHD, center shift, bigger engine) was lofty. In the context of other recent R-Type Continental sales, this is a reasonable result.


## Lot 110: 1963 Lotus Elite SE


Gooding Christie's


**Sold for $81,200**


*Chassis no. US64EB1921; Engine no. FWA40076885. Black with silver roof over black vinyl. Older restoration, #2- condition.*


**Equipment:** RHD. 1216cc/75hp Coventry Climax four-cylinder, dual Webers, ZF four-speed, Borrani wire wheels, Pirelli Cinturato tires, woodrim steering wheel, dual Raydot mirrors, tool roll.


**Condition:** Desirable SE package and ZF gearbox. An older restoration from the 1980s but still very pretty. Good paint. The panel gaps are probably better than when the car was new. Lovely interior other than yellowing rubber on the shift boot.


**Bottom line:** The Elite marked a great leap forward for Lotus, with the company moving from kit and race car builder to proper road car manufacturer. With a full fiberglass monocoque, the Elite was clever but costly and fragile. But it was also light, at about 1100 pounds, handsome, and quick. More than 1000 were built before Colin Chapman debuted the more profitable Elan. In terms of collectibility, Elites with the Special Equipment (SE) package/ZF gearbox are sought after, while RHD cars typically come at a discount on this side of the pond. This one brought well under its $100K low estimate, but all things considered $81K is perfectly fair.


## Lot 106: 1953 Chrysler Special by Ghia


Gooding Christie's


Gooding Christie's


Gooding Christie's


**Sold for $257,600**


*Chassis no. 7236150. Light gray over dark red leather. Unrestored original, 4+ condition.*


**Equipment:** 331cid/180hp Chrysler V-8, column shift automatic, wire wheels, whitewalls, pushbutton radio.


**Condition:** Represented as one of 16 built and eight remaining. Formerly owned by jockey Johnny Longden. With the same owner since 1979 and kept largely original. Sound but dull and chipped paint. Tired brightwork. There are mounting holes on the bottom front for a set of steel bumper guards that an owner installed in the 1950s. Scratches in the windshield. Cracked weatherstripping. Very well-preserved original upholstery. Cracks in the steering wheel rim. An interesting piece of Virgil Exner design and the fruitful partnership between Chrysler and Ghia. Preserve or restore? It could really go either way.


**Bottom line:** The various Ghia-bodied Chrysler specials from the 1950s are some of the most striking cars of their era, so restoration would arguably be the appropriate move here. There’s no way to do it economically, though, and the buyer here didn’t exactly get the car for a steal.


## Lot 145: 1957 Alfa Romeo Giulietta Sprint Veloce Alleggerita


Gooding Christie's


**Sold for $280,000**


*Chassis no. AR1493E*03559*; Engine no. AR1315*30279*. Bianco Spagna over red, black vinyl. Older restoration, #2- condition.*


**Equipment:** 1290cc/90hp, four-speed, hub caps, Pirelli Cinturato tires, side curtains.


**Condition:** Represented as one of approximately 40 remaining out of 200 originally built. Period hill climb and rally history. Spent most of its life in Switzerland. Original engine and restored in original colors. Dull bumpers and headlight bezels. Beautiful shiny wheels, though the hub caps look like older originals. Mild pitting on the trunk handle. Lightly scratched window frames. A sharp Alfa with competition specs.


**Bottom line:** The *Alleggerita* (“lightened”) model was built on the already potent and chuckable Giulietta Sprint Veloce, but with aluminum doors, hood, trunk lid, bumpers, and headlight bezels, as well as a more spartan interior and Plexiglas windows. Less weight usually means more money in the world of sports cars, of course, so on the rare occasion that an *Alleggerita* does come up for sale, it can be worth almost twice as much as a standard Sprint Veloce model.


Bonhams sold this example in 2013 for £113,500 (about $171K at the time) and Gooding Christie’s estimated $325,000–$400,000 for it in 2026. It crossed the block at no reserve to quite a bit less than that, another example of ’50s and ’60s cars in Monterey this year looking sleepy while the modern stuff makes the headlines.


## Lot 55: 1967 Porsche 910


Gooding Christie's


**Sold for $1,655,000**


*Chassis no. 910020; Engine no. 910044. White with light blue stripe, red seats. Competition restoration, #3+ condition.*


**Equipment:** LHD. 2.0L flat-six, five-speed, centerlock wheels, Momo Prorotipo steering wheel.


**Condition:** One of 27 Porsche 910s built. Raced throughout 1969 by Vic Elford, Bill Bradley, John Fitzpatrick, Tory Dean, Gijs van Lennep. First in class at the 1969 Spa 1000Km, 12th overall at Nürburgring. Disassembled but retained by the original owner for 30 years, later restored. Has since run at Goodwood Revival and Le Mans Classic. Restoration from the 1990s and repainted a few years ago. Scratched headlight covers and windshield wiper. Scratched right taillight bezel. Worn driver’s seat. For a race car, it looks excellent.


**Bottom line:** This 910 was a $2.3M no-sale at Broad Arrow’s Porsche 75th Anniversary sale in 2023, which was probably the best time and place to move a historic racer like this. At Pebble Beach, it simply wasn’t a standout, but the seller decided to let it go.


## Lot 68: 1993 Vector Avtech WX-3R Roadster Prototype


Gooding Christie's/Mike Maez


**Sold for $346,000**


*Chassis no. 1V9VW2620PW048002. Amethyst Purple over two-tone purple leather. Unrestored original, #3+ condition.*


**Equipment:** 6.0L/625hp twin-turbo V8, automatic, Pirelli P Zero tires, fire system, alligator pattern seat inserts, digital screens.


Gooding Christie's/Mike Maez


**Condition:** The only example built and the only open-top Vector ever made. Featured in company promo materials and owned by Vector founder Jerry Wiegert until 2019. Showing chips and cracks on the nose, as well as two large cracks behind the driver’s seat and another large one on the engine cover. Clean interior, with maybe the widest sills I’ve ever seen. Paint flaws take nothing away from this car’s charisma and cool factor.


**Bottom line:** Sold for $500,000 at RM Sotheby’s Phoenix auction in 2019 and was an $850,000 no-sale at RM Sotheby’s Monterey two years ago. So, not all modern exotics are getting more expensive in 2026. This car has uniqueness and outrageousness going for it, but two high-profile auction appearances in recent memory water down the outrageousness somewhat.


## Lot 136: 2004 Porsche 911 GT3


Gooding Christie's


**Sold for $351,500**


*Chassis no. WP0AC29914S692126. Speed Yellow over black leather. Original, #2 condition.*


**Equipment:** 3600cc/385hp flat-six, six-speed, yellow calipers, manuals, tool kit, jack.


**Condition:** Showing 9789 miles. Approximately $64,000 in service and detailing recently performed, and the 2025 Porsche Classic National Preservation and Restoration Challenge winner. Flawless paint and bodywork, the engine compartment looks like new. The only flaws are the minor wrinkles to the seat upholstery. A truly exceptional example of an early GT3.


**Bottom line:** The 996-generation 911 was the first to see the now immensely popular GT3 package, but the 996 version has also traditionally been the least expensive way to get a GT3 badge, and prices for it have been somewhat quiet relative to the rest of the 911 world. This is an exceptional example, though, and two bidders were smitten enough to bid it up to twice its $175K high estimate. We’ll have to look for more 996 GT3 sales to see if this is an outlier or a breakout sale for the model.


## Lot 146: 1930 Packard 734 Speedster Runabout


Gooding Christie's


**Sold for $1,765,000**


*Engine no. 184092. Dark green with tan cloth top over tan leather. Older restoration, #1 condition.*


**Equipment:** Straight-eight, three-speed, chrome wire wheels, Firestone blackwall tires, dual sidemount spares, Goddess of Speed mascot, wood dash, Jaeger dash clock.


**Condition:** One of 39 boattail runabouts produced. First in class at Pebble Beach in 2006, Timeless Beauty award at Amelia Island in 2007, and first in class at the Kirkland Concours. Previously owned by notable collectors Otis Chandler, Ray Sherr, and Ralph Stein. An older concours restoration that still looks incredible today. There is not a flaw of note to be seen anywhere on this car.


**Bottom line:** It speaks to the quality of the restoration and the careful ownership of this car that it still looks showable 20 years after the work was performed. The Model 734 Speedster was one of the more overtly sporting and expensive American cars money could buy, costing $5000 at a time when you could buy a new Ford for about a tenth of that. The Speedster Runabout is also the most desirable body style fitted to the 734 platform, and others have sold in recent years for similar prices to this one.


## Lot 20: 1959 Maserati Tipo 61 Birdcage by Allegretti


Gooding Christie's


**Sold for $4,240,000**


*Chassis no. 2452; Engine no. 2454. White and blue over blue. Older restoration, #3+ condition.*


**Equipment:** RHD. 2890cc/250hp straight-six, dual Webers, four-speed, side exhaust, painted Borrani wire wheels, Dunlop Racing tires, woodrim steering wheel, roll bar.


**Condition:** The first of just 17 Tipo 61s and just 22 Birdcages total built. Raced on the West Coast from 1959 through 1963 and scored victories at Palm Springs, Willow Springs, Vaca Valley, Santa Barbara, Oakland, Pomona, Reno, and Laguna Seca. Both Jim Hall and Ken Miles drove it in period. Restored in the 1970s. With the same owner since 1998, and used at select historic events. Retains its original chassis and body. Currently fitted with a replica engine, but a period block is included in the sale. Good older paint with a few cracks, chips, and touch-ups. Used interior. A historic Maserati, very usable.


**Bottom line:** The Tipo 60/61 is commonly referred to as the Birdcage thanks to its partially exposed spaceframe chassis made up of about 200 chromoly tubes welded together. It was also the last Maserati sports car to have significant top-level racing success, until the MC12 in the 2000s. This Birdcage sold in Monterey in 1998 for $937,500, which was good value at the time relative to Maseratis of similar vintage and performance. And in 2026, $4.2M is also good value relative to Ferraris of similar vintage and performance.


## Lot 188: 1966 Ferrari 275 GTS


Gooding Christie's/Mike Maez


**Sold for $1,820,000**


*Chassis no. 07929; Engine no. 07929. Red over red leather. Unrestored original, #4+ condition.*


**Equipment:** 3286cc/260hp V-12, five-speed, centerlock alloy wheels, boot cover, woodrim steering wheel, wood dash, Voxson radio, books, tools.


**Condition:** Originally finished in Grigio Fumo (Smoke Gray) and sold new in Italy. In California by 1970 and has been with the same Southern California family since 1981. Drivetrain removed in the early 1990s and rebuilt, then stored alongside the car until earlier this year, when it was finally reinstalled. Dull, chipped and cracked ancient repaint. Original interior with worn and lightly cracked leather, tired-looking carpets, and faded, dirty gauges. Engine looks clean and fresh, a stark contrast to the rest of the car, while the underbody is original but has clearly benefited from a dry, Western climate. Something of a barn find, but not the crusty, rusty kind.


Gooding Christie's/Mike Maez


Gooding Christie's/Mike Maez


**Bottom line:** There aren’t too many undiscovered classic Ferraris left, but they are still out there, and for a certain type of collector they are exciting. Two such collectors must have been paying attention to this car at Pebble Beach, because its high estimate was $1.2M. Freshly restored 275 GTSs have sold for way less than this.


## Lot 135: 1961 Ferrari 250 GT SWB Berlinetta Competizione


Gooding Christie's


**Sold for $8,090,000**


*Chassis no. 2701GT; Engine no. 4039. Red over blue leather with gray cloth inserts. Older restoration, #3- condition.*


**Equipment:** 2053cc/280hp V-12, triple Webers, four-speed, Borrani wire wheels, dual Talbot Berlin mirrors, woodrim steering wheel, Veglia gauges.


**Condition:** Period history includes the 1967 Targa Florio (DNF). In the U.S., minus its original engine, by the 1970s, and at one point even had an American V-8 in it. Restored in the 1980s using a 250 GTE engine built to competition specs. Regularly historic-raced since. Showing a ton of paint chips on the nose and numerous cracks throughout. Dirty wheels. Clean interior. A little beat up, but it’s a race car.


**Bottom line:** This SWB doesn’t have a noteworthy race history, was wrecked in period, and doesn’t have its original engine. Today, it’s showing plenty of wear and tear from an active life as an event car. Given all that, it sold for a very soft price. But “very soft” in the world of these Ferrari competition cars still means 8 million bucks, below the model’s condition #4 (fair) value in our price guide.


## Lot 44: 1968 Porsche 907 Langheck


Gooding Christie's


**Sold for $3,305,000**


*Chassis no. 907005. White and yellow, red seats. Older restoration, #2- condition.*


**Equipment:** RHD. 2.2L flat-eight, five-speed, centerlock wheels, Dunlop Racing tires.


**Condition:** First overall at the 1968 24 Hours of Daytona, making it the first Porsche to win a 24-hour race. Second overall at Monza that year, too. Run by privateers at Le Mans and was a DNF. Restoration work in the 1990s and 2010s. Presents beautifully enough for a race car, with some scratches and cracks in the back window being the only major issue.


**Bottom line:** It’s hard to believe that Porsche went from the pocket-sized four-cylinder 718 to the all-conquering flat-12–powered 917 in just a decade, but it did, and the 907 falls somewhere in the middle of that meteoric rise. It used essentially the same steel tubular monocoque as the 910 that preceded it but with a curvy (and delightfully pretty) new body, and it incorporated either the six-cylinder engine from the 906 or the 2.2-liter Type 771 flat-eight.


This one has history and glorious looks going for it, so it’s a bit of a surprise that bidding was relatively sleepy. For reference, this car actually sold for more than this ($3.63M) in Amelia Island 12 years ago, and another 907 with less race history and less attractive short tail bodywork sold for €4,390,400 ($4,848,758) in 2022.


## Lot 31: 1966 Ferrari Dino 206 S Berlinetta


Gooding Christie's


**Sold for $2,975,000**


*Chassis no. 014; Engine no. 014. Red with blue and white stripe over red and blue. Visually maintained, largely original, #3 condition.*


**Equipment:** RHD. 2.0L V-6, Lucas fuel injection, center shift five-speed, yellow centerlock wheels, Veglia gauges.


**Condition:** The last of three Dino 206 S coupes produced by Drogo and campaigned by Luigi Chinetti’s North American Racing Team (NART), competing at Le Mans three times as well as Daytona, Watkins Glen, Sebring twice, plus the inaugural Can-Am series. Impressively preserved and largely original. The paint is aged and shows damage throughout with swirls, plus some chips across the door sills and quarter panels. The interior appears original, with chips and bumps to the finish. An absolutely beautifully styled race car with the battle scars to prove its history.


**Bottom line:** This is a gorgeous little car, like a miniature-scale 330 P3, and though its race results were mostly unremarkable, it ran many high-profile events during a golden age of sports car racing. Its completeness and its history count for a lot, but because it’s a Ferrari, that lower-displacement V-6 will always put it on a lower tier in terms of collectibility. The price here is well below the car’s $3.5M low estimate.


## Lot 26: 1963 Ferrari 250 P by Fantuzzi


Greg Ingold


**Sold for $18,705,000**


*Chassis no. 0810; Engine no. 0810. Red over blue.* Visually maintained, largely original, #2-.


**Equipment:** RHD. 3.0L V-12, five-speed with right-side shift, painted Borrani wire wheels, woodrim steering wheel, Veglia gauges.


**Condition:** The first P series Ferrari, debuted at Monza and raced by Scuderia Ferrari for the 1963 season, where it took second overall at the 12 hours of Sebring and third overall at the 24 hours of Le Mans. Later campaigned by NART in North America. In present ownership since 1988. Very good older paint, although there is a small spider crack on the right rear quarter panel, a chip on the left rear portion of the spoiler, and a filled chip on the right side of the nose. The wheel locks have peeling chrome. The spartan interior presents well, and while it shows wear from use, it is not overly worn. A beautiful and significant P series Ferrari.


**Bottom line:** The 250 P marked an important new direction for Ferrari, being the first Ferrari sports racer with a V-12 mounted behind the driver, and this is the first one of four built. It’s the only one to appear at auction in recent memory, and it has serious provenance and preservation. It all adds up to a deserved eight-figure price.


## Lot 39: 1964 Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe


[Greg Ingold](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/gregory-ingold/)


**Sold for $42,905,000**


*Chassis no. CSX2300. Guardsman Blue with white Le Mans stripes over black cloth. Older restoration, #2- condition.*


**Equipment:** 289cid V-8, quadruple Webers, four-speed, centerlock wheels, side exhaust, Nardi woodrim steering wheel, Smiths gauges.


**Condition:** The third of just six Cobra Daytonas produced, part of Shelby’s historic 1965 endurance racing run. Debuted at the Tour de France Automobile with Bob Bondurant and Jochen Neerpasch driving. Sixth overall at Daytona. Hit by a Volvo shortly after the start at Sebring but went on to finish 13th overall. Painted in Ford of France colors for the Nürburgring 1000Km and finished 12th overall. Ninth overall at Reims, and Shelby secured the 1965 FIA World Manufacturers’ Championship. Later raced in Japan through 1968, and was even used as a street car in Tokyo, powered by a milder Ford V-8 road engine. Purchased by Carroll Shelby in 1975 and was in his possession until 1998.


Restored in the past and retains excellent paint; only a couple of minor chips above the right fog light and on the wheel well lip behind the left rear tire suggest any real damage. Some discoloration at the exhaust tips does indicate use, but the overall presentation is excellent. The interior does present some wear to the seat upholstery, but nothing is overly worn. A near once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to purchase a real Shelby Daytona. The last time a Cobra Daytona coupe was offered publicly was in 2009 at Mecum Auctions here in Monterey, where CSX2601 sold for $7,685,000. That was 17 years ago.


**Bottom line:** Despite all the huge prices for modern Ferraris at the 2026 Monterey auctions, this 62-year-old Ford-powered racer was the highlight car of the week, earning a bigger price than anything else and in the process becoming the most expensive American car ever sold at auction. Two phone bidders duked it out well past the “in excess of $25,000,000” estimate and put up Ferrari 250 GTO money. The new owner is reported to be U.S.-based.
